pages.text: Three little pigs left home to build their very own houses.
The first pig was lazy and built his house from straw.
The second pig built his house from sticks and branches.
The third pig worked hard and built his house from bricks.
A hungry wolf came along and knocked on the straw door.
The wolf huffed and puffed, and the straw house fell down.
The pig ran fast to his brother's house made of sticks.
The wolf huffed again, and the stick house fell down too.
Both pigs ran to their brother's strong house made of bricks.
The wolf huffed with all his strength, but the house stood firm.
Tired and hungry, the wolf finally left the forest for good.
The three pigs learned that careful work always pays off.
A little girl always wore a warm red hooded coat.
One day, her mother asked her to bring cakes to grandma.
The girl walked alone along the path through the big forest.
A clever wolf found her and asked where she was going.
The wolf ran ahead and reached grandma's house first.
The wolf hid grandma away and put on her clothes instead.
The girl arrived and noticed the strange voice and big eyes.
A woodcutter passing by heard strange noises from the house.
The woodcutter rushed in and chased the frightened wolf away.
They found grandma hidden safe and sound inside the closet.
Everyone was happy and shared the cakes together at the table.
The girl learned to never talk to strangers in the forest.
A fast hare loved to tease the slow tortoise every day.
Tired of the jokes, the tortoise challenged the hare to a race.
All the forest animals came to watch the big race.
At the signal, the hare shot off and got far ahead.
The hare looked back and laughed at the slow tortoise.
So sure of winning, the hare decided to rest under a tree.
The hare fell fast asleep, sure he had plenty of time.
The tortoise kept walking slowly, but he never once stopped.
Step by step, the tortoise got closer and closer to the finish.
The hare woke up suddenly and ran as fast as he could.
But it was too late, the tortoise had crossed the line first.
Everyone learned that slow and steady can also win the race.
A little girl with golden hair walked alone through the forest.
She found a small house and went in since the door was open.
On the table sat three bowls of warm soup waiting.
She tasted the first, but it was much too hot.
She tasted the second, but it was much too cold.
The third bowl was just right, and she ate it all.
Then she tried three chairs, but only the small one felt comfy.
She sat down hard, and the little chair broke apart.
Tired now, she went upstairs and tried three different beds.
The small bed was just right, and she fell fast asleep.
The bear family came home and found everything all messed up.
The girl woke up scared, said sorry, and ran home fast.
In the hot summer, an ant worked hard gathering food every day.
A grasshopper spent his days singing and dancing in the sun.
The grasshopper laughed at the ant for working so hard.
The ant kept carrying grains back to her safe little burrow.
Slowly, summer ended and a cold wind began to blow.
Winter arrived with snow, and the grasshopper had no food left.
Hungry and cold, the grasshopper knocked on the ant's door.
The ant opened the door and saw her sad, hungry friend.
Kindly, the ant shared the food she had carefully saved.
The grasshopper thanked her warmly and promised to plan ahead too.
The next spring, the two friends worked together happily.
They learned that planning ahead and helping others is always good.
A woman baked a sweet gingerbread man and put him in the oven.
When she opened the oven, he jumped out and started to run.
"You can't catch me!" he shouted, running down the road.
The woman chased after him, but he was much too fast.
A dog tried to catch him, but he kept on running.
A cow tried too, but she could never quite reach him.
He came to a wide river and did not know how to cross.
A clever fox offered to carry him across on her back.
The fox swam slowly, saying the water was getting deeper.
He climbed onto her nose so he would not get wet.
At that moment, the fox opened her mouth with a quick snap.
The gingerbread man learned, too late, not to trust clever strangers.
Little Sara was always afraid to speak in front of the class.
Her hands would shake whenever she had to present a project.
Sara's grandmother gave her a small round golden mirror.
"This mirror always shows someone brave," grandma said with a smile.
Sara looked into the mirror and saw only her own face.
"But I only see myself," Sara said, puzzled by the answer.
"Exactly," grandma replied. "Courage already lives inside you."
The next day, Sara carried the mirror hidden in her pocket.
Before speaking, she quickly glanced at her brave reflection.
She took a deep breath, smiled, and began to speak slowly and clearly.
The class clapped, and Sara's heart filled with pride.
Sara learned that courage doesn't come from outside, but from within.
In the neighborhood lived Tom, a boy full of good ideas.
One day he saw an elderly neighbor struggling with heavy bags.
Tom ran over and helped carry the bags to her door.
The neighbor smiled and thanked him with a slice of homemade cake.
Tom realized that helping others made him feel truly happy.
He decided to start a club with friends to help the neighborhood.
They made a colorful poster and called it the Helping Hands Club.
Every week, the group helped someone different around the neighborhood.
They watered plants, walked dogs, and helped tidy the park.
The neighbors began to smile more and talk to each other more.
The neighborhood became a friendlier place thanks to the little club.
Tom learned that small acts of help can change the world around us.
Little Nuno was always very busy, running from place to place.
He rushed to school, to games, and to his friends' houses.
But Nuno began to feel more and more tired and a little confused.
His grandfather noticed and invited him to sit together in the garden.
"Close your eyes and listen," grandpa said in a soft voice.
Nuno heard the birds singing and the wind moving through the leaves.
Then grandpa asked, "What do you feel, right now?"
Nuno thought for a moment and said, "I feel tired, but also calm."
"That is your inner voice," grandpa explained gently.
"It always knows what you need, if you stop to listen."
From that day on, Nuno paused every afternoon to breathe quietly.
He learned that knowing his own feelings helped him feel happier.
Little Iris thought she was too young to help anyone at all.
One day, her grandfather gave her a small bag of sunflower seeds.
"Plant a seed every time you do something kind," he said.
Iris helped a classmate pick up the pencils that had fallen.
That afternoon, she planted her very first seed in the little garden.
The next day, she helped set the table without being asked.
She planted another seed and smiled watching the garden grow.
Weeks passed, and Iris kept doing small, kind little gestures.
She helped neighbors, shared toys, and listened to sad friends.
The garden filled up with tall sunflowers shining in the sun.
Iris's friends also began to be kinder to one another.
Iris realized that kindness, like seeds, grows when it is shared.
